claim: Lenticular fiber cells are comprised of extremely long-lived proteins while still maintaining an active biochemical state.
source: The lenticular fiber cells are comprised of extremely long-lived proteins while still maintaining an active biochemical state.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing 14N/15N ratios and biochemical activity.

claim: Dysregulation of biochemical activities in lenticular fiber cells has been implicated in diseases such as age-related cataracts.
source: Dysregulation of these activities has been implicated in diseases such as age-related cataracts.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific understanding about cataracts.

claim: 248 lens proteins were measured for 14N/15N-peptide ratios.
source: We measured the 14N/15N-peptide ratios of 248 lens proteins, including Crystallin, Aquaporin, Collagen and enzymes that catalyze glycolysis and oxidation/reduction reactions.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Direct comparison of lens cortex versus nucleus revealed little or no 15N-protein contents in most nuclear proteins.
source: Direct comparison of lens cortex versus nucleus revealed little or no 15N-protein contents in most nuclear proteins, while there were a broad range of 14N/15N ratios in cortex proteins.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data comparing cortex and nucleus.

claim: There were a broad range of 14N/15N ratios in cortex proteins.
source: Direct comparison of lens cortex versus nucleus revealed little or no 15N-protein contents in most nuclear proteins, while there were a broad range of 14N/15N ratios in cortex proteins.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Many enzymes with relatively high abundance in nucleus were exceedingly long-lived, like Crystallins.
source: Unexpectedly, like Crystallins, many enzymes with relatively high abundance in nucleus were also exceedingly long-lived.
evidence: This is an unexpected finding from the experimental data showing high 14N/15N ratios for enzymes.

claim: The slow replacement of long-lived enzymes in spite of young age of mice suggests their potential roles in age-related metabolic changes in the lens.
source: The slow replacement of these enzymes in spite of young age of mice suggests their potential roles in age-related metabolic changes in the lens.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings about enzyme longevity.

claim: The lens consists of an outer capsule of type IV collagen-laminin membrane, the cortex of lens epithelium, and denuclearized and organelle-free fiber cells at the core.
source: It consists of an outer capsule of type IV collagen-laminin membrane, the cortex of lens epithelium, and denuclearized and organelle-free fiber cells at the core.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about lens structure.

claim: A single layer of germinal cells beneath the anterior capsule gives rise to transitional cells which differentiate into elongating fiber cells and finally the mature lenticular fiber cells forming the nuclear mass of the lens.
source: A single layer of germinal cells beneath the anterior capsule gives rise to transitional cells which differentiate into elongating fiber cells and finally the mature lenticular fiber cells forming the nuclear mass of the lens.
evidence: This describes the established developmental process of lens fiber cells.

claim: The human lens continues to grow slowly in its weight and size throughout life.
source: In this process, the human lens continues to grow slowly in its weight and size throughout life (Vavvas et al., 2002; Guirou et al., 2013; Augusteyn, 2007; Bassnett, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Lens disease, such as cataracts, account for approximately half of the global blindness.
source: Frequently associated with aging, lens disease, such as cataracts, account for approximately half of the global blindness (the World Health Organization data).
evidence: This is supported by World Health Organization data.

claim: The underlying molecular mechanisms for most cataracts remain poorly understood.
source: However, the underlying molecular mechanisms for most cataracts remain poorly understood (Pescosolido et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation indicating the current state of knowledge.

claim: Accumulation of oxidized proteins and lipids predisposes the lens to nuclear cataract development.
source: Evidence suggest that accumulation of oxidized proteins and lipids predisposes the lens to nuclear cataract development (Reddy, 1971; Williams, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Despite the slow turnover of the lens tissue, it remains a site of biochemical activity.
source: Despite the slow turnover of the lens tissue, it remains a site of biochemical activity (Reddy and Giblin, 1984; Hejtmancik et al., 2015), in which the production of reducing metabolites and perhaps local enzymatic reactions within the fiber cells are important in combating oxidative stress.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The production of reducing metabolites and perhaps local enzymatic reactions within the fiber cells are important in combating oxidative stress.
source: Despite the slow turnover of the lens tissue, it remains a site of biochemical activity (Reddy and Giblin, 1984; Hejtmancik et al., 2015), in which the production of reducing metabolites and perhaps local enzymatic reactions within the fiber cells are important in combating oxidative stress.
evidence: This is supported by citations and involves some speculation about enzymatic reactions.

claim: Radiocarbon (14C) dating studies demonstrated that with respect of the total protein and lipid, there was little turnover at the nuclear core of lens.
source: Previously, radiocarbon (14C) dating studies demonstrated that with respect of the total protein and lipid, there was little turnover at the nuclear core of lens (Lynnerup et al., 2008; Hughes et al., 2015; Nielsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous radiocarbon dating studies.

claim: A recent single-fiber-cell transcriptome study of postnatal day 2 mice detected mRNA encoding proteins known to exist in anucleate lens fibers.
source: However, a recent single-fiber-cell transcriptome study of postnatal day 2 mice detected mRNA encoding proteins known to exist in anucleate lens fibers (Gangalum et al., 2018), implicating active protein synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a transcriptome study.

claim: Detection of mRNA encoding proteins in anucleate lens fibers implicates active protein synthesis.
source: However, a recent single-fiber-cell transcriptome study of postnatal day 2 mice detected mRNA encoding proteins known to exist in anucleate lens fibers (Gangalum et al., 2018), implicating active protein synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited transcriptome study.

claim: Mice were fed with exclusively 15N chow between 3 and 15 weeks of age.
source: Between 3 and 15 weeks of age, mice were fed with exclusively 15N chow (Savas et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2018), following which the eye tissues were harvested.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: 535 proteins were identified at 1% FDR at the protein level in the entire lens.
source: In total, 535 proteins were identified at 1% FDR at the protein level, of which 248 proteins showed the presence of both fully 14N and 15N spectra for calculating their 14N/15N ratios (MS1 ratios of the old vs. the new protein. See Methods, Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: 14N/15N ratios reflected the proportions of individual proteins being replaced with new 15N proteins in addition to newly formed fiber layers being added to the growing lens.
source: These ratios reflected the proportions of individual proteins being replaced with new 15N proteins in addition to newly formed fiber layers being added to the growing lens.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the 14N/15N ratios represent.

claim: More than 50% of individual proteins in the lens were only detected in their 14N forms.
source: More than 50% of individual proteins in the lens were only detected in their 14N forms, as compared to 1.8% and 2.8% in the vitreoretinal and sclera/choroid tissues respectively (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 1.8% of individual proteins in the vitreoretinal tissue were only detected in their 14N forms.
source: More than 50% of individual proteins in the lens were only detected in their 14N forms, as compared to 1.8% and 2.8% in the vitreoretinal and sclera/choroid tissues respectively (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 2.8% of individual proteins in the sclera/choroid tissue were only detected in their 14N forms.
source: More than 50% of individual proteins in the lens were only detected in their 14N forms, as compared to 1.8% and 2.8% in the vitreoretinal and sclera/choroid tissues respectively (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Non-lens tissues had a majority of individual proteins completely replaced by new 15N proteins.
source: These non-lens tissues had a majority of individual proteins completely replaced by new 15N proteins, in contrast to the slow turnover of 1.7% of individual lens protein.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data comparing lens and non-lens tissues.

claim: 1.7% of individual lens proteins showed complete replacement by new 15N proteins.
source: These non-lens tissues had a majority of individual proteins completely replaced by new 15N proteins, in contrast to the slow turnover of 1.7% of individual lens protein.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Extremely long-lived proteins in the lens included structural proteins such as PE-binding protein 1 (PEBP-1), β-Catenin, and Moesin.
source: These extremely long-lived proteins included structural proteins such as PE-binding protein 1 (PEBP-1), β-Catenin, Moesin, and enzymes that are involved in oxidoreduction such as Peroxiredoxin-2 (Prdx2), Farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (FPS) and Aldehyde dehydrogenase (Aldh7A), and in glycolysis such as ATP-dependent 6-phosphofructokinase (ATP-PFK).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing absence of 15N labels for these proteins.

claim: Extremely long-lived proteins in the lens included enzymes involved in oxidoreduction such as Peroxiredoxin-2 (Prdx2), Farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (FPS) and Aldehyde dehydrogenase (Aldh7A).
source: These extremely long-lived proteins included structural proteins such as PE-binding protein 1 (PEBP-1), β-Catenin, Moesin, and enzymes that are involved in oxidoreduction such as Peroxiredoxin-2 (Prdx2), Farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (FPS) and Aldehyde dehydrogenase (Aldh7A), and in glycolysis such as ATP-dependent 6-phosphofructokinase (ATP-PFK).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing absence of 15N labels for these proteins.

claim: Extremely long-lived proteins in the lens included enzymes involved in glycolysis such as ATP-dependent 6-phosphofructokinase (ATP-PFK).
source: These extremely long-lived proteins included structural proteins such as PE-binding protein 1 (PEBP-1), β-Catenin, Moesin, and enzymes that are involved in oxidoreduction such as Peroxiredoxin-2 (Prdx2), Farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (FPS) and Aldehyde dehydrogenase (Aldh7A), and in glycolysis such as ATP-dependent 6-phosphofructokinase (ATP-PFK).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing absence of 15N labels for these proteins.

claim: Lens proteins exhibited the most long-lived proteins with greater 14N proportions among proteins with both 14N and 15N peptides detected.
source: For those proteins with both 14N and 15N peptides detected, lens proteins exhibited the most long-lived proteins with greater 14N proportions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Histone variant H3.3 was among the fastest turned over proteins with 14N/15N = 0.2.
source: Meanwhile, the histone variant H3.3 was among the fastest turned over proteins (14N/15N = 0.2, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: H3.3 is associated with transcription loci in the chromosome.
source: H3.3 is associated with transcription loci in the chromosome (Szenker et al., 2011; Toyama et al., 2013) and its frequent replacement by newer H3.3 indicated active transcription and translation activities in the lens, most likely in the capsule and the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Frequent replacement of H3.3 by newer H3.3 indicated active transcription and translation activities in the lens, most likely in the capsule and the cortex.
source: H3.3 is associated with transcription loci in the chromosome (Szenker et al., 2011; Toyama et al., 2013) and its frequent replacement by newer H3.3 indicated active transcription and translation activities in the lens, most likely in the capsule and the cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on H3.3 turnover combined with cited knowledge.

claim: Histone H3.1 and H3.2 in the heterochromatin regions only renew during cell cycle replication.
source: By contrast, histone H3.1 and H3.2 in the heterochromatin regions that only renew during cell cycle replication (Hake and Allis, 2006) were found to be comprised of a greater proportion of older proteins (14N/15N = 2.98 and 4.02, respectively), consistent with the notion that most lens fiber cells are postmitotically differentiated and subsequently lose chromatin (Bassnett and Mataic, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Histone H3.1 and H3.2 were found to be comprised of a greater proportion of older proteins (14N/15N = 2.98 and 4.02, respectively).
source: By contrast, histone H3.1 and H3.2 in the heterochromatin regions that only renew during cell cycle replication (Hake and Allis, 2006) were found to be comprised of a greater proportion of older proteins (14N/15N = 2.98 and 4.02, respectively), consistent with the notion that most lens fiber cells are postmitotically differentiated and subsequently lose chromatin (Bassnett and Mataic, 1997).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The greater proportion of older H3.1 and H3.2 proteins is consistent with the notion that most lens fiber cells are postmitotically differentiated and subsequently lose chromatin.
source: By contrast, histone H3.1 and H3.2 in the heterochromatin regions that only renew during cell cycle replication (Hake and Allis, 2006) were found to be comprised of a greater proportion of older proteins (14N/15N = 2.98 and 4.02, respectively), consistent with the notion that most lens fiber cells are postmitotically differentiated and subsequently lose chromatin (Bassnett and Mataic, 1997).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental data with cited knowledge about lens fiber cell differentiation.

claim: The overall rate of lens cell growth was estimated to be slow, with 1/5 to 1/4 of H3.2 and H3.1 being synthesized with full 15N during the 12 week period.
source: The overall rate of lens cell growth was estimated to be slow, with 1/5 to 1/4 of H3.2 and H3.1 being synthesized with full 15N during the 12 week period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data for H3.1 and H3.2 turnover rates.

claim: The beaded filament proteins of Phakinin and Filensin are implicated in cataract development.
source: However, in these fiber cells that had ceased to replicate, the beaded filament proteins of Phakinin and Filensin (Blankenship et al., 2001; Wenke et al., 2016) that are implicated in cataract development (Conley et al., 2000; Jakobs et al., 2000; Carter et al., 2000) were still being actively produced (14N/15N equals 2.02 and 1.02 respectively) (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Phakinin and Filensin were still being actively produced in fiber cells that had ceased to replicate (14N/15N equals 2.02 and 1.02 respectively).
source: However, in these fiber cells that had ceased to replicate, the beaded filament proteins of Phakinin and Filensin (Blankenship et al., 2001; Wenke et al., 2016) that are implicated in cataract development (Conley et al., 2000; Jakobs et al., 2000; Carter et al., 2000) were still being actively produced (14N/15N equals 2.02 and 1.02 respectively) (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: γ-Crystallins A/E/F/N that are localized to the nuclear lens showed the greatest proportion of their 14N-proteins (14N/15N > 20).
source: The γ-Crystallins A/E/F/N that are localized to the nuclear lens showed the greatest proportion of their 14N-proteins (14N/15N > 20), followed by phosphoglycerate mutase 2 (Pgm2) that catalyzes glycolysis (14N/15N > 20), and cysteine protease Calpain-3 (14N/15N = 18.8) responsible for protein degradation (Figure 2D).

claim: Phosphoglycerate mutase 2 (Pgm2) that catalyzes glycolysis had 14N/15N > 20.
source: The γ-Crystallins A/E/F/N that are localized to the nuclear lens showed the greatest proportion of their 14N-proteins (14N/15N > 20), followed by phosphoglycerate mutase 2 (Pgm2) that catalyzes glycolysis (14N/15N > 20), and cysteine protease Calpain-3 (14N/15N = 18.8) responsible for protein degradation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cysteine protease Calpain-3 responsible for protein degradation had 14N/15N = 18.8.
source: The γ-Crystallins A/E/F/N that are localized to the nuclear lens showed the greatest proportion of their 14N-proteins (14N/15N > 20), followed by phosphoglycerate mutase 2 (Pgm2) that catalyzes glycolysis (14N/15N > 20), and cysteine protease Calpain-3 (14N/15N = 18.8) responsible for protein degradation (Figure 2D).

claim: Crystallins are the most abundant proteins in the lens.
source: Crystallins are the most abundant proteins in the lens (Figure 1D), and they are divided into α, β and γ protein groups based on sequence homology.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and is established knowledge about lens composition.

claim: Crystallins are divided into α, β and γ protein groups based on sequence homology.
source: Crystallins are the most abundant proteins in the lens (Figure 1D), and they are divided into α, β and γ protein groups based on sequence homology.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Crystallin classification.

claim: α- and β- Crystallins (Crya and Cryb) are chaperone proteins for protein refolding under conditions of oxidative stress.
source: α- and β- Crystallins (Crya and Cryb) are chaperone proteins for protein refolding under conditions of oxidative stress (Hejtmancik et al., 2015; Horwitz et al., 1999; Andley, 2007), and the densely packed γ-Crystallins (Cryg) contribute to reflection and hardness of the lens.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The densely packed γ-Crystallins (Cryg) contribute to reflection and hardness of the lens.
source: α- and β- Crystallins (Crya and Cryb) are chaperone proteins for protein refolding under conditions of oxidative stress (Hejtmancik et al., 2015; Horwitz et al., 1999; Andley, 2007), and the densely packed γ-Crystallins (Cryg) contribute to reflection and hardness of the lens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about γ-Crystallin function.

claim: A range of 14N/15N ratios was detected among distinct family members of each Crystallin class: from 1.4 to 3.01 for α-Crystallins, 1.16 to 9.13 for β-Crystallins, and 1.46 to >20 for γ-Crystallins.
source: Interestingly, a range of 14N/15N ratios was detected among distinct family members of each class (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1): from 1.4 to 3.01 for α-Crystallins, 1.16 to 9.13 for β-Crystallins, and 1.46 to >20 for γ-Crystallins.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The range of 14N/15N ratios among Crystallin family members is in agreement with previous analysis of Crystallin longevity in aged rats.
source: These results are in agreement with our previous analysis of Crystallin longevity in aged rats (Toyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: Cataract-linked mutations have been reported in structural proteins including those forming the connexin gap junction channel and aquaporin water channel.
source: Beside the Crystallins, cataract-linked mutations have been reported in other structural proteins (Shiels et al., 2010; Churchill and Graw, 2011), including those forming the connexin gap junction channel (Berthoud and Ngezahayo, 2017; Goodenough, 1992) and aquaporin water channel (Agre and Kozono, 2003) (A complete list of all identified proteins in Supplementary file 1 with selected examples shown in Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Cx50 was among the longest-lived gap junction proteins with an 14N/15N ratio of 7.19.
source: In our dataset, Cx50 was among the longest-lived gap junction proteins with an 14N/15N ratio of 7.19, consistent with Cx50's presence in mature fibers at the nucleus (White et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Cx50's long-lived nature is consistent with Cx50's presence in mature fibers at the nucleus.
source: In our dataset, Cx50 was among the longest-lived gap junction proteins with an 14N/15N ratio of 7.19, consistent with Cx50's presence in mature fibers at the nucleus (White et al., 1992).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental data with cited knowledge about Cx50 localization.

claim: The water channel Aquaporin Aqp0/Lim1/Mip had 14N/15N = 1.34.

claim: The water channel Lim2/MP19/Cataract19 had 14N/15N = 3.25.

evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Gap junctions and Aquaporins form channels known to be critical for the passage of important small metabolites to the lens.
source: These gap junctions and Aquaporins form channels known to be critical for the passage of important small metabolites to the lens, and mutations of their genes predispose individuals to cataracts (Verkman et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2011; Chepelinsky, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mutations of gap junction and Aquaporin genes predispose individuals to cataracts.
source: These gap junctions and Aquaporins form channels known to be critical for the passage of important small metabolites to the lens, and mutations of their genes predispose individuals to cataracts (Verkman et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2011; Chepelinsky, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The outer capsule of the lens resembles other basement membranes such as the glomerular basement membrane of the kidney.
source: Unlike the mature fibers that uniquely form the core of the lens, the outer capsule of the lens resembles other basement membranes such as the glomerular basement membrane of the kidney.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Mutations in the major components of type IV Collagen cause Alport syndrome that concurrently affects the kidney, the eye including cataracts and the ear.
source: Mutations in the major components of type IV Collagen cause Alport syndrome that concurrently affects the kidney, the eye including cataracts and the ear.

claim: Type IV Collagen proteins in the lens membrane matrix are produced by the adjacent epithelial cells.

evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the measured ratios to other lens proteins.

claim: Collagen IV-α1, -α2 and -α3 turnover rates in the lens were remarkably similar to their counterparts in the kidney at 1.43, 1.43 and 1.16 respectively.

claim: Perlecan/Hspg2 at the outer and inner surfaces contributes to anionic charges.

claim: The slow replacement of Perlecan may contribute to the gradual loss of its sulfated glycosaminoglycan moieties during aging.
